# We Read It So You Don't Have To

Dense source material should become clear without losing its qualifications.

## Purpose

We Read It So You Don't Have To turns consequential primary material into a
clear, faithful account. It saves the reader time by finding what changed and
preserving the qualifications needed to understand the effect.

Every article answers:

1. What happened?
2. Why does it matter?
3. What are the three key takeaways?

## Reader expectation

The article must link to the source when possible and point readers to the
passages behind its important claims.

By the end, the reader should understand the source's practical effect and the
limits of what it establishes.

## What belongs

- Research papers.
- SEC filings and other consequential regulatory disclosures.
- Earnings reports and calls.
- Legislation, regulations, and official guidance.
- Court opinions and important filings.
- API documentation and material technical changes.
- Terms of service, privacy policies, and other agreements with meaningful consequences.
- Audits, investigations, standards, and public reports that require close reading.

The source must carry enough public consequence or explanatory value to justify the reader's attention.

## What does not

- A summary based on a press release when the primary document is available.
- Routine documents with no meaningful change or consequence.
- Commentary on a source the writer did not read in full.
- A cherry-picked clause presented without the surrounding rule, exception, or definition.
- A document whose only appeal is that it is long or difficult.
- Breaking news that can be explained accurately without sustained document work.
- Original data reporting that belongs in Research.

## Typical length

Most articles run from 900 to 1,800 words. A narrow policy or documentation change may need 600 to 900. A major ruling, filing, or body of legislation may require more space, along with a clearly labeled guide to the relevant provisions.

The three takeaways should be concise enough to remember and substantial enough to carry the story.

## Tone

Use plain language and keep the seriousness of the source. A light line can
relieve needless technical friction, provided it leaves the meaning intact.

Define technical terms on first use. When exact wording matters, put it beside
the plain explanation.

## Publishing philosophy

Read the complete relevant source, including notes, appendices, and material
references. Give page numbers, sections, docket entries, or stable anchors so
another editor can retrace the work. Quote only the language the reader needs.

Explain what the document establishes, what it claims, and what the writer infers. Those are different categories and should read differently. A company's filing can establish that the company made a claim. Further evidence is required to establish that the claim is true.

Compression must preserve qualifications. If a caveat changes the meaning of a finding, it belongs in the article. When the document changes after publication, retain the version reviewed or record the access date and update the story as needed.

## Success metric

Fidelity and time saved are the central measures. A successful article lets a busy reader understand the source's consequences while giving a specialist a reliable path back to the evidence.

In editorial review, check whether:

- the three takeaways match the source;
- every material statement can be traced to a precise location;
- qualifications survive the summary;
- facts, claims, and interpretation remain distinct;
- a reader can explain the practical effect after one reading;
- errors are uncommon, and corrections are prompt and explicit.

Completion data may reveal where readers lose the thread. The stronger test is whether readers can accurately state what the document changes and where the answer came from.

## Internal examples

- A court opinion changes how an online practice is treated. Give the holding,
  who it affects, and the questions the court left open.
- An earnings filing shows that a celebrated product remains a small part of
  the company's business. The relevant numbers explain the gap.
- Compare two versions of a privacy policy after it adds a new category of data
  use. Quote the operative clause and state any jurisdictional limit.
- API documentation restricts a capability used by independent developers.
  Identify the affected use cases and migration window from the documentation
  itself.

## Anti-examples

- A paper reduced to the most surprising sentence in its abstract.
- An earnings story that repeats adjusted figures without explaining the measure.
- A legal ruling described through a party's press statement.
- A terms-of-service update covered from a screenshot with no version comparison.
- Three takeaways that restate the same point.
- A confident practical conclusion the source does not support.
- A long article that leaves the reader unable to say what changed.
